interactive.title: Percentage change
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in twelve small screens on a percentage bar, the starting amount lined up with 100% and the change at its end, some showing an idea and the rest asking you to try it.

explain.text:
A percentage change compares a change with the amount you started from. Find the change, new minus original, then write it as a fraction of the original and turn that into a percentage. So a load rising from 40 A to 50 A has changed by 10 A, and 10 ÷ 40 × 100 = 25%, a rise of 25%. A fall gives a negative change, so £250 falling to £200 is −50 ÷ 250 × 100 = −20%, which is the same as a 20% fall. You can also divide the new amount by the original to get the multiplier. 50 ÷ 40 = 1.25, which is 125% of the start, and taking off the 100% you started with leaves the 25% change.

The slips are about what you divide by and what you report. Dividing by the new amount compares the change with the wrong whole, so the £50 fall would come out as 25% of £200 instead of 20% of £250. That is why 40 A up to 50 A is a 25% rise, while 50 A down to 40 A is only a 20% fall. Stopping at 125%, or at 80% for a fall, is a common slip, since that is the new amount as a share of the old, not the change. When the amounts are themselves percentages, the plain gap between them is in percentage points, so a pass rate going from 40% to 50% is up 10 percentage points, which is a 25% rise.

**Percentage change is the change ÷ the original × 100. Divide by where you started, read a minus sign as a fall, and call the gap between two percentages percentage points.**

practice.text:
**Rule of thumb:** Take the original from the new amount to get the change, divide by the original and times by 100. A minus sign means a fall.

**Worked example:** A 64 A load falls to 48 A. The change is 48 − 64 = −16 A. Then −16 ÷ 64 = −0.25, and −0.25 × 100 = −25%, a 25% fall. As a check, 48 ÷ 64 = 0.75, so the new load is 75% of the start, 25% down.

**Common mistakes**
- Dividing by the new amount. £160 up to £200 is a £40 rise, and 40 ÷ 160 × 100 = 25%, not 40 ÷ 200 × 100 = 20%.
- Reporting the share instead of the change. 68 ÷ 80 = 0.85 says the new price is 85% of the old, so the change is −15%.
- Reading the change itself as the percentage. A £40 rise is not a 40% rise. It is 40 ÷ 160 × 100 = 25%.
- Mixing up percentage points and percent. A pass rate going from 50% to 60% is up 10 percentage points, but 10 ÷ 50 × 100 = a 20% rise.
